You are going to turn a protocol into a Rhylthyme program: parallel **tracks** of sequential **steps**, each with a duration and a start trigger, that one person follows against a live clock.

Plan this as a Rhylthyme protocol and deliver a live timeline: Sandwich ELISA on Two Plates, One Washer for two 96-well plates, staggered 30 minutes
Resource limits: one plate washer, one 37 °C incubator holding two plates, one plate reader, one operator.
No finishing time was given; finish as early as the work allows.

Source text (read all of it):
<<<
Sandwich ELISA on Two Plates, One Washer

Two 96-well plates are run half an hour apart through a sandwich ELISA for a secreted cytokine. There is one automated plate washer, one 37 °C plate incubator that holds two plates, one plate reader and one operator. The washer is the bottleneck: no two plates can be in it at once, and every incubation is bracketed by a wash.

Day 1
1. Coat plate 1 with 100 µL per well of capture antibody in carbonate buffer, seal it and leave it in the cold room at 4 °C overnight. Take it out when you are ready to start, not before.
2. Coat plate 2 the same way half an hour later, so the two plates stay half an hour apart all day.

Day 2, reagents
3. Fifteen hours into the coat, make up the seven-point standard curve in assay diluent; 30 minutes.
4. Dilute the samples 1:4 into assay diluent and lay out the plate map; 30 minutes.

Day 2, plate 1
5. Wash the plate four times with 300 µL of wash buffer; 5 minutes on the washer.
6. Block with 200 µL per well of assay diluent for 1 hour at 37 °C.
7. Wash four times; 5 minutes on the washer.
8. Add 100 µL of standards and samples and incubate for 2 hours at 37 °C. Nothing goes on the plate until the dilutions are laid out.
9. Wash four times; 5 minutes on the washer.
10. Add 100 µL of biotinylated detection antibody and incubate for 1 hour at 37 °C.
11. Wash four times; 5 minutes on the washer.
12. Add 100 µL of TMB substrate, develop in the dark for exactly 15 minutes and stop with 50 µL of 2 N sulfuric acid.
13. Read the absorbance at 450 nm with a 570 nm reference; 5 minutes on the reader.

Day 2, plate 2
14. Wash plate 2 four times as soon as the washer is free; 5 minutes.
15. Block plate 2 with 200 µL of assay diluent for 1 hour at 37 °C.
16. Wash plate 2 again once plate 1 is off the washer; 5 minutes.
17. Add the standards and samples to plate 2 and incubate for 2 hours at 37 °C.
18. Wash plate 2; 5 minutes.
19. Add the detection antibody to plate 2 and incubate for 1 hour at 37 °C.
20. Wash plate 2 a final time; 5 minutes.
21. Develop plate 2 with TMB for exactly 15 minutes and stop it.
22. Read plate 2 at 450 nm; 5 minutes.
>>>

Read all of it before you answer. Then say back, in one paragraph and in your own words: what is being made, for how many (or at what scale), by when, and under what constraints — equipment that exists only once, how many people are working, anything that has to be held, rested or ready at a particular moment. If the text you were given looks truncated, or points at a section that is not here, say so instead of filling the gap.

End your reply with the same read-back as JSON in a single ```json fenced block:

  "deadline": "2026-11-26T18:00:00",
  "constraints": ["one oven", "two burners", "two cooks"]
}
```

**Read-back**

This is not a thing being made so much as a two-plate sandwich ELISA measuring a secreted cytokine in two 96-well plates, run by a single operator, with the second plate deliberately lagging the first by 30 minutes all the way through. Day 1 is just the coat: capture antibody in carbonate buffer on plate 1, sealed into the 4 °C cold room overnight, and plate 2 coated the same way 30 minutes later so the two plates hold their half-hour offset for the rest of the run. Day 2 opens with reagent prep — a seven-point standard curve in assay diluent and a 1:4 dilution of the samples with the plate map laid out, 30 minutes each, started roughly fifteen hours into the coat — and from there each plate runs the same five-block sequence: wash ×4 (5 min), block 1 h at 37 °C, wash, standards/samples 2 h at 37 °C, wash, biotinylated detection antibody 1 h at 37 °C, wash, TMB develop in the dark for exactly 15 min and stop with 2 N sulfuric acid, then read at 450 nm with a 570 nm reference (5 min). The binding constraints are equipment and hands: one automatic plate washer (the stated bottleneck — no two plates in it at once, and *every* incubation is bracketed by a wash, so each plate's washes queue behind the other's), one 37 °C incubator that holds both plates (so incubations overlap, but only two plates' worth), one plate reader, and one operator, meaning every manual step serializes. Things that must be held or ready at a moment: the plate 1 coat must be out of the cold room only when actually starting; the 15-hour coat→prep interval; the standards/samples dilutions must exist before anything goes onto either plate ("nothing goes on the plate until the dilutions are laid out"); and the 15-minute TMB development in the dark is a hard exact timer. No deadline was given — the instruction is to finish as early as the work allows — so the only fixed clock relationships are the 15 h coat→reagent-prep offset and the 30-minute plate-to-plate stagger. Nothing in the supplied text looks truncated: Day 1 (2 steps), Day 2 reagents (2 steps) and the full 18-step Day 2 sequence for both plates are all present, though the wash for plate 2 after its block is explicitly gated on plate 1 being off the washer.

Day 1 is the overnight 4 °C capture-antibody coat (plate 1, then plate 2 half an hour later); Day 2 starts about fifteen hours into the coat with 30 min of standard-curve preparation and 30 min of 1:4 sample dilution plus plate mapping, then each plate runs wash ×4 (5 min), 1 h block at 37 °C, wash, 2 h standards/samples at 37 °C, wash, 1 h detection antibody at 37 °C, wash, exactly 15 min TMB development in the dark stopped with 2 N sulfuric acid, and a 5 min 450/570 nm read. Constraints: one plate washer (the bottleneck — no two plates at once, and every incubation is bracketed by a wash, so washes must queue), one 37 °C incubator holding at most two plates, one plate reader, and one operator, so all hands-on work serializes; the dilutions must be laid out before anything is added to a plate, the coat plate comes out of the cold room only when the run starts, and the 15-minute TMB step is a hard exact timer. No deadline or finishing time was given — finish as early as the work allows.",

  ]

```

**The model, restated**

A Rhylthyme program is a set of **tracks**, and each track is one strictly sequential line of work: its steps run one after another and never overlap, so anything that must happen *while* something else is running has to live in its own track. Every **step** carries exactly one duration kind — `fixed` with a `seconds` value, `variable` with `minSeconds`/`maxSeconds`/`defaultSeconds`, or `indefinite` (it ends when the person ends it, with a `defaultSeconds` so previews still look sane) — plus a `startTrigger` that anchors it either to the clock (`programStart`, `programStartOffset`) or to another step (`afterStep`, `afterStepWithBuffer`, optionally with `offsetSeconds`, `event` or a `choiceId` for branches), or to a human tap (`manual`), an abort (`onAbort`), or a combination (`compound` with `logic: all | any`). `stepId`s are global: unique across the entire program, not per track, and every `afterStep` must point at a step that exists and must not close a cycle. Any `task` a step occupies needs a matching `resourceConstraints` entry, and that entry's `maxConcurrent` is the thing that stops two steps from sharing the single washer, incubator or reader — `maxConcurrent: 2` on the incubator literally means "two plates fit in here". Work repeated n times — here, two plates run the same 30-minutes-apart sequence — is `replicates: {count, mode: "serial" | "parallel" | "stagger", delay}` on **one** step, never duplicated step JSON: the followers chain with `instances: "each"` to inherit the count and per-instance pairing, a `"all"` trigger becomes the barrier that waits for every instance, and `replicates.maxInFlight: k` is used when a *holding area* between the repetition and its barrier only fits k at a time, so the upstream step is held back rather than the downstream one being stranded. Shared, single-instance work — the once-only 15-hour coat, the standard curve, the sample dilutions — stays its own unreplicated steps, and cross-track `afterStep` references are how those gate the plate chains.

For the constraints: one **operator** (`actors: 1`) means all hands-on work serializes, but the real gate is the **washer** (`maxConcurrent: 1`) — the stated bottleneck, and since every incubation is bracketed by a wash, the two plates' washes must queue rather than overlap. The **37 °C incubator** holds both plates (`maxConcurrent: 2`), which is what lets plate 1's 2-hour sample incubation overlap plate 2's 1-hour block. The **reader** is single (`maxConcurrent: 1`), the **bench/manual pipetting** task is single because there is one person, the **dark space** for TMB development holds two plates (the develops are 30 min apart and last 15 min, so they never actually collide), and the **4 °C cold room** holds both coated plates overnight. I intend to model the two plates as one `replicates: {count: 2, mode: "stagger", delay: "30m"}` chain with `instances: "each"` followers, with the Day 2 reagent prep as separate single steps that the plate chains wait on.

```json
{
  "acknowledgement": "tracks are sequential lines of work whose steps never overlap; each step has exactly one duration kind (fixed/variable/indefinite) and one startTrigger (programStart, programStartOffset, afterStep, afterStepWithBuffer, manual, onAbort or compound); stepIds are unique across the whole program, not per track; every task a step occupies needs a matching resourceConstraints entry whose maxConcurrent is what serializes shared equipment; repeated work is replicates on one step (mode serial/parallel/stagger) with instances:'each' to chain per instance, instances:'all' as the barrier and replicates.maxInFlight:k when the holding area only fits k.",
  "resourceConstraints": [
    { "task": "washer", "maxConcurrent": 1, "note": "automated plate washer; the stated bottleneck — no two plates in it at once, and every incubation is bracketed by a wash" },
    { "task": "incubator", "maxConcurrent": 2, "note": "one 37 °C plate incubator that holds exactly two plates; lets plate 1's 2 h sample incubation overlap plate 2's 1 h block" },
    { "task": "reader", "maxConcurrent": 1, "note": "one plate reader; 5 min 450/570 nm read per plate" },
    { "task": "bench", "maxConcurrent": 1, "note": "manual pipetting, dilutions, plate map and acid stop — one operator, so all hands-on work serializes" },
    { "task": "darkbox", "maxConcurrent": 2, "note": "dark space for the exact 15 min TMB development; holds both plates, though the 30 min stagger means the develops never collide" },
    { "task": "coldroom", "maxConcurrent": 2, "note": "4 °C cold room for the overnight capture-antibody coat of both plates" }
  ],
  "actors": 1
}
```

Turn 4 of 4 — relationships, then the program.

Take the step list from turn 3 exactly as it stands.

**First, tracks.** Put each step in a track: one track per parallel line of work — per dish, per station, per instrument, per performer, per sample group. Steps in one track run one after another and must not overlap; anything that runs while something else runs belongs in its own track.

**Second, triggers.** Give every step a `startTrigger` from this vocabulary and no other:

- `{"type":"programStart"}` — at t = 0.
- `{"type":"programStartOffset","offsetSeconds":n}` — n seconds after the start; this is how a short track is delayed so it finishes with the others.
- `{"type":"afterStep","stepId":"x"}` — when x ends. Add `"offsetSeconds"` for a gap, `"event":"start"` to hang off x's start instead of its end, `"instances"` when x is replicated.
- `{"type":"afterStepWithBuffer","stepId":"x","bufferSeconds":n}` — n seconds after x ends.
